title: Planning Fallacy
description: People consistently underestimate the time, costs, and risks of a project they are directly involved in, while believing their current plan is realistic.
shortDescription: People consistently underestimate the time, costs, and risks of a project they are directly involved in, while believing their current plan is realistic.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: People consistently underestimate the time, costs, and risks of a project they are directly involved in, while believing their current plan is realistic.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A renovation that you estimate will take 2 weeks takes 2 months.
A work project is promised for Friday; it’s actually done next Wednesday.
A wedding budget that starts at $10,000 balloons to $18,000, and the couple insists “we didn’t see it coming.”

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Optimistic time lines despite past failures.
Dismissing outside‑view data (“This time is different”).

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “If nothing goes wrong, we’ll finish by…”
“That’s a worst‑case number; we’ll come in lower.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You haven’t looked at how long similar projects actually took others.
You respond to warnings with “Yeah, but this is simpler.”

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: When planning, we naturally focus on the unique features of our specific situation (inside view) and neglect base rates of similar past efforts (outside view). The optimism also feels motivating.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Use the “outside view”: find a reference class of similar projects and take the average completion time or cost as your baseline.
Add a 30–50% buffer to your initial estimate, even if it feels excessive.
Track your actuals vs. estimates over time; the data is humbling.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Doubling down after the first delay instead of recalibrating.
Treating the planning fallacy as a sign of incompetence rather than a universal cognitive trait.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A software team estimates a feature will take 3 weeks. Their manager asks, “How long did the last three features of similar size take?” Average: 7 weeks. The team insists this one is simpler. It ships in 8 weeks.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Your plan is a fantasy until you’ve checked it against what actually happened the last ten times. Use yesterday’s results, not today’s optimism.
